paras: The threatened lynching of Milt Parker was a reported threat against a Black man accused of assaulting a white girl near Bantam, Ohio, in late December 1888. A brief telegraphic dispatch said he would be lynched when caught, but the coverage reports no capture, attack or killing.

According to a dispatch datelined Bantam on December 28, Parker, described as "colored," committed "a criminal assault" on Efile Townson, "a respectable white girl," near the town on the previous Wednesday night, December 26. The dispatch stated the accusation as fact and named no source for it, whether officers, the girl's family or anyone else. It closed with the sentence "He will be lynched when caught," which indicates that Parker was still at large, though no search or mob is described.
No report of Parker's capture, arrest, trial or lynching was found in the coverage, and no later item mentions the case.

The story reached readers only as a one-sentence wire item in papers outside Ohio, in Pennsylvania and the District of Columbia. The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer ran it on December 28 among its "Telegraphic Taps," between an Italian powder-magazine explosion and a Tennessee shooting, with the names given as "Mitt Parker" and "Eddie Townson" and the ending "He will be lynched if caught." The Washington Evening Post printed the same dispatch the next day under the head "Will be Lynched When Caught," directly below an Omaha item about a man whipped for beating his wife.
Both papers identified the accused by race and the girl as white and "respectable," treated the assault as established, and presented the coming lynching as a matter of course, without comment.
The two printings differ in spelling, "Milt" and "Efile" in Washington against "Mitt" and "Eddie" in Lancaster, variants of the same dispatch that leave the correct names uncertain.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Milt Parker
bases: The only reports say the accused man 'will be lynched' when caught, a threat of lynching with no act by any group reported (A1, A2).

No one is reported killed: the wire item says only that Parker would be lynched when or if caught, naming no mob or group and reporting no capture (A1, A2). The threat rests on an accusation of criminal assault on a white girl (A1, A2).
Both items are the same brief telegraphic dispatch from Bantam, reprinted almost word for word, so they are one report rather than two independent ones (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Wire report from Bantam
accounts.gist: Parker, 'colored,' committed a criminal assault on a white girl near Bantam on Wednesday night and will be lynched when caught; the accusation is stated as fact without a named source.

framing.detail: The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer ran the item among its 'Telegraphic Taps,' presenting the assault as fact and the lynching as a likely outcome 'if caught.'
The Washington Evening Post gave it the head 'Will be Lynched When Caught,' stating the assault as fact and the lynching as a foregone conclusion.

conflicts.note: Both items are the same dispatch; the differences are probably typesetting or OCR variants, and neither is clearly better evidence.
